usage: I want to know the truth.
examples: 사실 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.
Actually, I cannot eat spicy food.
Actually, I did not go to work yesterday.
nuance: Sa-sil means a fact or the truth, but at the start of a sentence it works like the English word actually to gently introduce honest information.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 진짜 for very.

examples: I told my friend a secret.
You must not know the secret.
nuance: Bi-mil means a secret and pairs naturally with the verb 지키다 to keep, so Koreans often say 비밀을 지키다 when promising to stay quiet.
mistakes: Do not say 비밀 하다 as a verb.

nuance: Gyu-chik means a rule and usually takes the verb 지키다 to follow, so 규칙을 지키다 is the standard way to say obey the rules in Korean.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 법 for law.

usage: I want to fix a bad habit.
I have a habit of sleeping early.
examples: I have a habit of exercising every morning.
I changed my coffee drinking habit.
nuance: Seup-gwan means a habit and often appears with 있다 to have, as in 습관이 있다, while 고치다 to fix is used for breaking a bad one.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 버릇 in tone.

examples: My friend has a very lively personality.
Because our personalities differ, we sometimes argue.
nuance: Seong-gyeok means personality or character, and Koreans frequently say 성격이 좋다 to mean someone is kind, so it carries a warm social meaning.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 기분 for mood.

usage: I want to build my ability.
examples: That person has excellent working ability.
I am building my Korean ability.
Effort is more important than ability.
nuance: Neung-nyeok means ability or capability and pairs with 있다 to have or 키우다 to grow, often describing skills people develop over time through practice.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 가능 for possible.

examples: I made a mistake at work today.
It is a small mistake, so it is okay.
I made the same mistake again.
nuance: Sil-su means a mistake and works with 하다 to do, so 실수하다 means to make a mistake, which is gentler than the harsher word for a serious error.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 잘못 for wrongdoing.

examples: To succeed, you must keep trying.
I am happy I succeeded in business.
nuance: Seong-gong means success and combines with 하다 to do, so 성공하다 means to succeed, and it is the natural opposite of the word for failure.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 합격 for passing exams.

examples: At first I failed, but I tried again.
I learned a lot from failure.
It is okay to fail, so please try.
nuance: Sil-pae means failure and takes 하다 to do, so 실패하다 means to fail, and Koreans often use it kindly to say failing is a normal part of learning.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 실수 for small mistakes.

usage: I make an effort every day.
I put in a lot of effort.
If you try, you can do well.
examples: I make an effort to learn Korean.
Without effort there is no success.
nuance: No-ryeok means effort and pairs with 하다 to do, so 노력하다 means to make an effort, and it is a warm word often used to praise hard work.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 노동 for labor.

usage: I do not know the difference well.
examples: The price difference is too big.
Please find the difference between two photos.
nuance: Cha-i means a difference between two or more things and usually appears with 있다 to have or 나다 to occur, so 차이가 있다 means there is a difference.
mistakes: Do not confuse it with 차이점 for specific points.
